title: Shisha stitch
subtitle: A stitched frame that holds a small mirror to fabric
excerpt: Shisha stitch is a two-stage technique from Indian mirror embroidery. A foundation grid of thread is laid across the mirror to hold it in place, then a row of looped stitches is worked around the rim, catching the foundation on each pass to draw it tight and form a neat frame. The method works with both traditional mica mirrors and modern glass shisha discs.
sourceNotes: Traditional technique from Kutch and Sindh mirror embroidery (shisha bharat); widely documented in Western needlework references including Mary Thomas's Dictionary of Embroidery Stitches (1934, revised 1989) and Constance Howard's Embroidery and Colour (1976). Formation follows the standard foundation-grid and buttonhole-loop method.

content.text: Shisha stitch attaches small mirrors or mica discs to fabric using two stages. First, a foundation of straight stitches is worked across the mirror in a grid, crossing over its face. Second, a row of looped stitches is worked around the mirror's edge, each stitch catching under the foundation threads and passing over the working thread to form a firm, decorative frame. The mirror is held entirely by this stitched frame and does not require adhesive.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Stranded cotton, 3-4 strands; or perle cotton no 8

items.label: Fabric
items.value: Firm woven fabric such as cotton, wool, or canvas; loose weaves do not hold the mirror securely

items.label: Mirror
items.value: Round shisha glass or mica disc, typically 1.5-3 cm in diameter

items.label: Hoop
items.value: 10-15 cm embroidery hoop to keep fabric taut

content.text: Place the mirror face-up on the fabric. Hold it in position with a fingertip or a small piece of low-tack tape while beginning the foundation. Bring the needle up at the fabric next to the mirror's edge on one side, lay the thread across the face of the mirror, and take it back down into the fabric on the opposite side. Work two or three parallel stitches across the mirror in this direction.

Turn 90 degrees and work two or three more parallel stitches crossing over the first set. These crossing stitches hold the mirror in place and form the grid the looped stitches will later catch. All foundation stitches should lie flat against the mirror face and not slide off the edge.

Bring the needle up at the fabric edge close to the mirror, working your way around the rim. To make each frame stitch: slide the needle under the foundation grid threads from right to left (not through the fabric), then loop the working thread under the needle tip and pull through. This forms a small loop similar to a buttonhole stitch, lying against the mirror's edge and catching the foundation at the same time.

Work these looped stitches evenly all the way around the mirror, spacing them so the frame covers the mirror's edge without gaps. Each loop catches under the foundation stitches and anchors into the fabric. When the circle is complete, the last stitch links back into the first to close the frame neatly.

Secure the thread on the back of the fabric with a few small stitches. The mirror should now be firmly held and should not shift when the fabric is flexed gently. A second round of decorative stitching, such as straight stitches radiating outward from the frame, can be added once the mirror is secured.

items.symptom: The mirror shifts or falls out
items.cause: The foundation grid stitches are too loose, or the looped frame stitches do not catch the foundation firmly
items.fix: Lay the foundation stitches snugly across the mirror face without pulling them tight enough to bow the mirror. When working each looped stitch, make sure the needle passes under all the foundation threads before the loop is pulled closed.

items.symptom: The frame is lumpy or uneven around the rim
items.cause: The looped stitches are not evenly spaced, or some are catching the fabric at different distances from the mirror edge
items.fix: Mark evenly-spaced points around the mirror with a water-soluble pen before starting the frame row. Keep each fabric entry point the same distance from the mirror's edge throughout.

items.symptom: Thread shows on the face of the mirror from the foundation stitches
items.cause: The foundation stitches were placed too far from the mirror's edge and do not lie near the rim
items.fix: Start and end each foundation stitch as close to the mirror's edge as the fabric allows. The stitches should cross the mirror face but concentrate near the rim so the frame row covers them.
